newsitem.title: USA: Rivlin-US pay rising across board, but not rapidly.
newsitem.headline: Rivlin-US pay rising across board, but not rapidly.

text.p: Federal Reserve Board Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said Friday that American wages are rising broadly, but not rapidly, and again reiterated her surprise that tight labor markets are not resulting in higher prices.

In an upbeat address at an Emerging Issues Forum at North Carolina State University in Raleigh, N.C., Rivlin called the Fed's recent rate hike an "insurance policy" against overheating in an economy that shows no sign of running out of steam.
"Wages haven't been rising especailly rapidly, but they are beginning to move up and they're moving up all across the board," Rivlin said.
"But surprisingly, prices are not (rising), or not yet," she added.
Rivlin said the ability of companies to absorb wage increases and maintain good profits indicates that productivity is on the rise.
"It's probably increasing more than we're measuring, especially in the service industries where we don't know how to measure it very well," she said.

Expressing satisfaction at the Clinton administration's progress in cutting the federal budget deficit, which she helped to bring about in her former roles in the White House, Rivlin said she was optimistic that there would be a bipartisan deal to balance the budget by 2002.

But she said a balanced budget deal depends heavily on getting agreement to reduce the rate of increase in Medicare and Medicaid, "because it is those programs that are increasing. Nothing else is increasing very significantly."
Finding little or no "bad news" in the economy, Rivlin said it is the Fed's job to "keep the good news flowing" with the tools it has at its disposal.

"The danger now does not seem to be that this long recovery from the recession of the beginning of the decade will run out of steam," she said. "The danger is on the other side -- that the economy, if it continues at this rate and if unemployment keeps dropping, will overheat, will give us inflation down the line which could mean the end of the growth."
The Fed's quarter-point hike in short-term interest rates on March 25 was an "insurance policy" aimed at keeping the recovery going "on a sustainable basis," Rivlin said.
Looking at the future of the economy, Rivlin said higher productivity, promoted by better education and a higher savings rate, are the keys to a higher standard of living.
"If I had to choose two major things that would contribute most to the future standard of living through increasing productivity, I think they would be improving education and saving more," she said.
